report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is well-supported. Bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) than no bystander CPR. Multiple observational studies and meta-analyses indicate that any bystander CPR—including hands-only—roughly doubles the odds of survival compared with no CPR. Hands-only CPR has also been shown to be at least as effective as conventional CPR with rescue breathing for adult primary cardiac arrest, and its simpler technique reduces barriers, increasing the likelihood that bystanders will act. The American Heart Association notes that immediate CPR can double or triple a victim’s chance of survival. A Swedish nationwide review found that as hands-only CPR rates increased six-fold over 18 years, survival from OHCA improved, with any form of CPR doubling survival versus no CPR. A separate multivariable analysis confirmed that both standard and compression-only bystander CPR were associated with higher survival compared with no bystander CPR. Thus, the evidence consistently supports that bystander hands-only CPR improves survival outcomes relative to no intervention.
